facts: Encyclopaedia Britannica defines a novel as “an invented prose narrative of considerable length and a certain complexity that deals imaginatively with human experience,” usually through connected events involving people in a setting [Encyclopaedia Britannica, Novel].
The SFWA Nebula rules classify a novel as 40,000 words or more [SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules].
BISG publishes the BISAC Fiction Subject Headings list and accompanying subject codes for categorizing fiction books [Book Industry Study Group, Fiction].

sources.label: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Novel
SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules
Book Industry Study Group, Fiction

facts: IngramSpark’s trim-size matrix lists 5 × 8 in and 6 × 9 in among its paperback sizes; paperback binding is listed as Perfect Bound [IngramSpark, Trim Size Matrix].

sources.label: IngramSpark, Trim Size Matrix

facts: IngramSpark’s matrix lists 5 × 8 in and 6 × 9 in for hardcover formats, with Case Laminate, Digital Cloth, or Jacketed Cover options [IngramSpark, Trim Size Matrix].

sources.label: IngramSpark, Trim Size Matrix

facts: EPUB 3.3 is a W3C Recommendation that defines authoring requirements for EPUB publications, the digital-publication packaging format [W3C, EPUB 3.3].

sources.label: W3C, EPUB 3.3

facts: ACX gives the estimating rule 9,300 words ≈ 1 finished hour of audiobook audio; finished hours can be estimated as total words ÷ 9,300 [ACX, Two Ways to Estimate Your Word Count].

sources.label: ACX, Two Ways to Estimate Your Word Count

facts: International Thriller Writers describes a thriller as fiction or nonfiction centered on suspense, danger, conflict, and high stakes; examples include murder mystery, suspense, horror, action/adventure, espionage, true crime, and war-related fiction [International Thriller Writers, About ITW].

sources.label: International Thriller Writers, About ITW

facts: Romance Writers of America identifies two essential elements: a central love story and an emotionally satisfying, optimistic ending [Romance Writers of America, About the Romance Genre].

sources.label: Romance Writers of America, About the Romance Genre
sources.page: Definition / The Basics of the Genre

facts: Duke’s fantasy guide describes fantasy as a world in which magic, supernatural forces, or otherwise impossible events are treated as real; those speculative elements significantly shape conflict and consequences [Duke University Libraries, Getting Started—Fantasy Genre Guide].

sources.label: Duke University Libraries, Getting Started—Fantasy Genre Guide

facts: Mystery fiction is organized around an unsolved crime—often a murder—and an investigation intended to determine what happened, who did it, and how; clues, suspects, motives, and red herrings guide the reader toward a solution [Mystery Writers of America, Plotting].

sources.label: Mystery Writers of America, Plotting

facts: Jane Friedman describes literary fiction as a novel intentionally distinguished by the quality and craft of its writing; “literary” describes the work’s mode of execution and reader experience more than a fixed subject matter, so it can overlap with other genres [Jane Friedman, Genre].
BISG’s Fiction Subject Headings list provides the industry category-code framework used to classify fiction, including literary and genre categories [Book Industry Study Group, Fiction].

sources.label: Jane Friedman, Genre
Book Industry Study Group, Fiction

facts: SFWA’s James Patrick Kelly describes science fiction as fiction built around ideas or developments connected with science, technology, society, or the future—asking what could happen even if it has not happened yet [James Patrick Kelly, Making Monsters].

sources.label: James Patrick Kelly, Making Monsters (SFWA)

facts: MIT’s writing-process guide names four distinct stages: prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing [MIT Comparative Media Studies/Writing, Writing Process].

sources.label: MIT Comparative Media Studies/Writing, Writing Process

facts: George R. R. Martin contrasts writers who plan extensively before drafting with writers who begin from a seed and discover the story as it grows; he says he is primarily a gardener, though not without a plan [George R. R. Martin, A Winter Garden].

sources.label: George R. R. Martin, A Winter Garden

facts: Martin’s “architects” plan extensively before drafting and know the structure, sequence of events, and character movements before writing [George R. R. Martin, A Winter Garden].

sources.label: George R. R. Martin, A Winter Garden

facts: Martin’s “gardeners” begin with an idea or seed and let the story grow while writing; characters and situations can change in ways the writer did not originally anticipate [George R. R. Martin, A Winter Garden].

sources.label: George R. R. Martin, A Winter Garden

facts: Ingermanson’s Snowflake Method starts with a one-sentence story summary, expands it into a paragraph covering setup, major disasters, and ending, then develops major-character summaries and further story detail [Randy Ingermanson, The Snowflake Method].

sources.label: Randy Ingermanson, The Snowflake Method

facts: Scrivener’s corkboard presents scenes and chapters as index-card-like cards that can be rearranged while writing, providing a visual outline of the project [Literature & Latte, Organize Your Scrivener Project with the Corkboard].

sources.label: Literature & Latte, Organize Your Scrivener Project with the Corkboard

facts: Anne Lamott says that all good writers write “shitty first drafts”; the first draft is where ideas are allowed onto the page before later shaping [Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird].
Stephen King advises writing the first draft with the door closed and revising with the door open [Stephen King, On Writing].

sources.label: Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird
Stephen King, On Writing

facts: Lamott treats a bad first draft as a normal stage: writers put down a rough version so they can later produce a better second draft [Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird].

sources.label: Anne Lamott, Bird by Bird

facts: Hemingway’s Paris Review interview records daily writing counts of 450, 575, 462, 1,250, and 512 words in its discussion of writing routines [Ernest Hemingway, The Paris Review interview].
The examples show that a daily target is a controllable production measure rather than a universal creative rule [Ernest Hemingway, The Paris Review interview].

sources.label: Ernest Hemingway, The Art of Fiction No. 21 (The Paris Review)

facts: Hemingway’s recorded daily counts include 450, 575, 462, and 512 words—several examples near a 500-word planning pace [Ernest Hemingway, The Paris Review interview].

sources.label: Ernest Hemingway, The Art of Fiction No. 21 (The Paris Review)

facts: In an 1899 letter to Cloudesley Johns, Jack London wrote that he was doing “a thousand words per day, six days per week” [Jack London, Letter to Cloudesley Johns].

sources.label: Jack London, Letter to Cloudesley Johns

facts: NaNoWriMo’s challenge is a 50,000-word first draft in 30 days, which is approximately 1,667 words per day [NaNoWriMo, NaNo Prep 101].

sources.label: NaNoWriMo, NaNo Prep 101: A Six-Week Workshop and Resource Guide

facts: Stephen King describes a 2,000-word daily writing target and also frames it as roughly ten pages a day [Stephen King, On Writing].

sources.label: Stephen King, On Writing

facts: Trollope reports training himself to write 250 words every quarter of an hour; at that rate, 2,500 words is ten quarter-hours, or 2.5 hours of writing [Anthony Trollope, An Autobiography].
He says he normally wrote for three hours a day, which would be about 3,000 words at that rate [Anthony Trollope, An Autobiography].

sources.label: Anthony Trollope, An Autobiography

facts: Chuck Sambuchino’s Writer’s Digest table presents recommended word counts by category rather than one universal novel length; adult genre targets differ substantially from children’s targets [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: Writer’s Digest lists literary fiction at 80,000–89,999 words as an ideal target, with roughly 71,000–109,000 words broadly acceptable [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: Writer’s Digest lists mystery and thriller/suspense novels at about 80,000–89,999 words as an ideal target, with roughly 71,000–109,000 broadly acceptable [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: Writer’s Digest gives roughly 71,000–109,000 words as the broadly acceptable range for romance novels [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: Writer’s Digest lists science fiction at 100,000–115,000 words as an ideal target, with roughly 86,000–124,000 potentially workable; fantasy is listed at 100,000–115,000 ideal, with roughly 90,000–124,000 potentially workable [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: Writer’s Digest lists young adult novels at 55,000–79,999 words as generally recommended, with about 47,000 words as the lower edge [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: Writer’s Digest lists middle-grade novels at 40,000–55,000 words [Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books].

sources.label: Chuck Sambuchino, Word Count for Novels and Children’s Books (Writer’s Digest)

facts: SFWA’s Nebula rules define a short story as fewer than 7,500 words [SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules].

sources.label: SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules

facts: SFWA’s Nebula rules define a novelette as at least 7,500 words but fewer than 17,500 words [SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules].

sources.label: SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules

facts: SFWA’s Nebula rules define a novella as at least 17,500 words but fewer than 40,000 words [SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules].

sources.label: SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules

facts: SFWA’s Nebula rules define a novel as 40,000 words or more [SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules].

sources.label: SFWA, Nebula Awards Rules

facts: Stephen King’s revision advice is to write the first draft with the door closed, then rewrite with the door open—private generation followed by reader-facing revision [Stephen King, On Writing].

sources.label: Stephen King, On Writing

facts: Purdue OWL defines reverse outlining as creating an outline after drafting: summarize each paragraph’s main point, explain its relation to the thesis or overall argument, and use the result to find gaps, repetition, or weak organization [Purdue OWL, Reverse Outlining].

sources.label: Purdue OWL, Reverse Outlining

facts: Jane Friedman’s beta-reader questionnaire asks readers what they liked and disliked, where they lost interest, whether the story grabbed them at the beginning, and whether the ending satisfied them [Jane Friedman, What to Ask Your Beta Readers].

sources.label: Jane Friedman, What to Ask Your Beta Readers

facts: King gives the rule of thumb “2nd Draft = 1st Draft − 10%,” treating a revision pass as an opportunity to remove unnecessary material [Stephen King, On Writing].

sources.label: Stephen King, On Writing

facts: King’s “2nd Draft = 1st Draft − 10%” formula describes a revised draft as a leaner version of the first draft, not merely a corrected copy [Stephen King, On Writing].

sources.label: Stephen King, On Writing

facts: The Editorial Freelancers Association distinguishes developmental editing, line editing, copyediting, and proofreading as different scopes from big-picture content through final production errors [Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions].

sources.label: Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions

facts: EFA defines developmental editing as work on content, organization, and overall structure or argument, often including plot, pacing, character arcs, point of view, and audience considerations in fiction [Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions].

sources.label: Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions

facts: EFA defines line editing as sentence- or paragraph-level work improving language, style, clarity, flow, tone, voice, and word choice while respecting the author’s intent [Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions].

sources.label: Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions

facts: EFA defines copyediting as checking correctness, consistency, and adherence to a style guide, including grammar, spelling, punctuation, usage, cross-references, and consistency [Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions].

sources.label: Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions

facts: EFA defines proofreading as the final check for production errors after layout or typesetting, including typos, formatting problems, and errors introduced during production [Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions].

sources.label: Editorial Freelancers Association, Editorial Service Definitions

facts: Shunn’s classic manuscript format specifies 12-point Times New Roman (or 12-point Courier when a publisher specifically requests Shunn Classic), double-spaced text, and one-inch margins [William Shunn, Classic Manuscript Format].

Shunn’s format uses a header with author surname, abbreviated title, and page number, plus left-aligned text, ragged right margin, and first-line paragraph indents [William Shunn, Classic Manuscript Format].

sources.label: William Shunn, Classic Manuscript Format
William Shunn, Classic Manuscript Format, p. 4

facts: Jane Friedman’s publishing-path chart distinguishes traditional publishing, self-publishing, and hybrid/author-funded arrangements by who pays, who controls rights, and how publication services are delivered [Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths].

sources.label: Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths: 2025–2026

facts: In Friedman’s traditional path, the publisher generally acquires the manuscript, pays production and distribution costs, and typically works through an agent; the author receives an advance and royalties but gives up some control [Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths].

sources.label: Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths: 2025–2026

facts: In self-publishing, the author acts as publisher, pays publication costs, hires or manages editorial/design/production services, and retains rights and control [Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths].
The fetched KDP help material lists a 70% eBook royalty option for a $2.99–$12.99 list-price band, with a 35% option outside the applicable 70% conditions [Amazon KDP, eBook Royalties].

sources.label: Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths: 2025–2026
Amazon KDP, eBook Royalties
sources.flag: page shell; rate text from indexed help extract

facts: Hybrid publishers put their name on the book and become publisher of record, but accepted authors fund publication; the author pays costs, signs a contract, and receives royalties, with packages and costs varying by publisher [Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths].

Friedman gives $25,000 as a rule-of-thumb estimate for some hybrid publication costs, while warning that packages may exclude print runs, developmental editing, marketing, or promotion [Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths].

sources.label: Jane Friedman, The Key Book Publishing Paths: 2025–2026
